name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,168

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: A virgin bride, apparently, is novel

blocks.note: first meaning: a bride is traditionally dressed in the colour of purity, so to all appearances she is one
second meaning: Wilkie Collins's 1859 sensation novel, without its opening article

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a supposedly chaste bride is something new.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like an adjective meaning new; it is the noun naming Wilkie Collins's mystery. 'Apparently' flags that the first reading is about how the bride looks.
explanation.definitionFit: Collins's famous Victorian mystery thriller carries this title, and a bride wearing traditional pale wedding dress fits the description literally.

clue.text: He loved Bosie in a natural state, they say

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than read, so the sound counts, not the spelling

blocks.note: untamed, living in nature, as animals or plants are

explanation.surface: A lover of Bosie is described as living in an untamed, natural way.
explanation.walkthrough: Bosie was Lord Alfred Douglas, whose affair with the playwright led to his trial and imprisonment; the surname is said exactly like the word for untamed.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde's passionate relationship with Lord Alfred Douglas, nicknamed Bosie, is among literature's most famous love affairs.

clue.text: Reminder for Lettie Colston: send out memoir to men

indicators.note: to send something out is to dispatch it in all directions, scattering the order

explanation.surface: A woman is told to post her memoir off to a group of men.
explanation.walkthrough: Lettie Colston is a character in Muriel Spark's novel of that title, in which elderly people receive anonymous calls saying 'Remember you must die'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase names a reminder of death, the very message Spark's anonymous caller keeps delivering to Dame Lettie.

clue.text: Criminal Genet’s refusal left one church tense

blocks.note: Jean Genet was French, so his 'no' is the French word

explanation.surface: Genet, a thief turned writer, turned something down, then walked out of a church in a tense state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Criminal Genet' reads as one phrase, since Genet really was a convicted thief; 'Criminal' is the definition, the Latin legal phrase for something not lawful.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin legal tag means 'it is not permitted', describing an act forbidden by law, hence unlawful or illegal.

clue.text: It was her beast twice seen in Finch’s home

definitions.note: a description of a person rather than a synonym

indicators.note: something seen within a place is placed inside it

blocks.note: a small bird such as a finch lives in one
the prefix meaning two or twice, as in biannual

explanation.surface: A woman's animal has been spotted twice at a Finch family house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' is the Psammead, the sand-fairy of Five Children and It; 'Finch' suggests To Kill a Mockingbird but is just a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: E. Nesbit created the grumpy wish-granting sand-fairy known as It, so the creature belonged to her as its author.

clue.text: End of file deleted in restore? Bloody computer!

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so just that one is used
deleting removes something, so that letter is struck out from within the word

blocks.note: the last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A user loses a file during a restore and swears at the machine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bloody' reads as a British curse, but here it is literal: the computer in 2001: A Space Odyssey murders the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: HAL 9000, the shipboard intelligence in Kubrick and Clarke's film, kills astronauts, so it is murderous in the literal sense.

clue.text: Book by Dylan Thomas, his first: a natural novel

indicators.note: a man's first, after his name, is the opening letter of that name
something novel is new, so the letters are made into a new arrangement

blocks.note: the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: A book by the Welsh poet Dylan Thomas, his debut, is called a natural novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dylan Thomas' reads as the poet's full name, but the definition stops at 'Dylan': Bob Dylan's experimental prose book. 'Thomas' only supplies its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan wrote the stream-of-consciousness prose poetry collection Tarantula in the mid-1960s, published in 1971.

clue.text: Theatre reworking Goethe with leads from La Bohème

indicators.note: leads are the front-runners, so the opening letters of each word are taken
to rework something is to make it over again in a different form

blocks.note: the opening letters of both words

explanation.surface: A theatre stages a new version of Goethe, borrowing stars from a Puccini opera.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a staging of Faust with singers from La Bohème; the playhouse is Shakespeare's on London's Bankside.
explanation.definitionFit: The Globe is the Elizabethan playhouse where Shakespeare's company performed, rebuilt on the South Bank in 1997.

clue.text: Murdoch, who’s no Romeo, enthrals southern goddess

indicators.note: a person who has none of something lacks it, so it is taken away
to enthral is to hold captive, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: R in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Murdoch, plainly no great lover, captivates a goddess from the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No Romeo' reads as a jibe about Murdoch's love life; it means drop the letter R from her first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Isis is the Egyptian mother goddess of magic and healing, wife of Osiris and mother of Horus.

clue.text: Writer of The Little Foxes or Lord of the Flies?

blocks.note: first meaning: the American playwright Lillian, author of the 1939 drama
second meaning: Beelzebub, lord of the flies, is a devil, a man from the underworld

explanation.surface: A question about who wrote one of two famous titles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lord of the Flies' looks like Golding's novel, but here it is the translation of Beelzebub; the question mark signals the playful second reading as a fellow from the infernal regions.
explanation.definitionFit: Lillian Hellman wrote The Little Foxes, and split in two her surname describes a demon from the underworld.

clue.text: Sailors at sea in a water-covered world

indicators.note: to be at sea is to be confused and disoriented, out of order

explanation.surface: Mariners on the ocean of a planet covered by water.
explanation.walkthrough: The planet in Stanisław Lem's novel is covered by a sentient ocean, so 'at sea' fits the surface picture and also signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: In Lem's science fiction novel, the planet's entire surface is a single thinking ocean studied by human scientists.

clue.text: Environmental writer with Catholic guilt, I’m told

indicators.note: being told something means hearing it spoken, so the sound is what counts

blocks.note: Graham Greene, whose novels are steeped in Catholic sin and conscience

explanation.surface: An eco-writer who also wrestles with Catholic guilt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Environmental writer' reads as one phrase; the definition is the first word alone, and the writer is the novelist of The Power and the Glory, whose surname is said the same.
explanation.definitionFit: The colour word is the everyday label for policies, products and people concerned with protecting the natural world.

clue.text: Asteroid 5099’s one with excellent nitrogen deposits

blocks.note: A1, first-rate, with the digit read as the letter I
deposits as in sand or mud banked up, or money placed in a bank

explanation.surface: An astronomer notes that a numbered asteroid has rich nitrogen deposits.
explanation.walkthrough: The minor planet 5099 was named after the Scottish novelist, author of The Wasp Factory and the Culture science fiction series.
explanation.definitionFit: Astronomers named minor planet 5099 in honour of the Scottish writer, so the asteroid bears his full name.

clue.text: “— Jones made his money in mines, And although he has left us his fame still shines” (William Gay)

definitions.text: “— Jones made his money in mines, And although he has left us his fame still shines” (William Gay)

blocks.clueFragment: “— Jones made his money in mines, And although he has left us his fame still shines”
blocks.note: surface reading: a comic couplet about a wealthy mine-owner whose first name is missing
setter's reading: the source names the poet whose verse supplies the missing forename

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: the gap is the forename of the mining magnate the verse commemorates.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is the man's Christian name, an apostle's name, completing the opening line of Gay's couplet.

clue.text: Financially, East Egg folk boggle my noodle

indicators.note: something that boggles the mind throws it into confusion

explanation.surface: Someone says the wealthy set of East Egg baffle their brain.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Great Gatsby, East Egg houses the inherited-wealth families like the Buchanans, while Gatsby's West Egg is newly rich. 'Noodle' is slang for the head.
explanation.definitionFit: Fitzgerald sets established families with inherited fortunes in East Egg, contrasting them with the self-made rich across the bay.

clue.text: Poetry-writing cop hides gall after being sacked

indicators.note: a sacked town is ransacked and left in disorder

explanation.surface: A policeman who writes verse keeps his bitterness hidden after losing his job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sacked' reads as dismissed, fitting the cop; the sense used is plundered and thrown into disarray.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Dalgliesh, P. D. James's Scotland Yard detective, is also a published poet in the novels.

clue.text: Bed-bound writer for Time to cover America

indicators.note: to cover something is to go around it, so these letters wrap the next ones

explanation.surface: A housebound journalist is hired by Time magazine to report on America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time' looks like the magazine, fitting the reporter picture; it is just the letter T, wrapped around the country with PRO in front.
explanation.definitionFit: Marcel Proust wrote much of In Search of Lost Time in bed in a cork-lined room, chronically ill.

clue.text: Freak about drugs? Not as much as Holmes’s bowing!

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing the bowing

indicators.note: to turn about is to face the other way, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Holmes was a drug fiend, then jokes that his violin playing was worse.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface nods to Holmes's cocaine habit; in the stories Watson complains of the detective scraping idly at his violin without melody.
explanation.definitionFit: Watson describes Holmes drawing discordant, melody-free sounds from his violin while thinking, so his playing lacked any recognisable air.

clue.text: Half of a B. S. Johnson book entertains nurse from LA

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a person from the city

indicators.note: a host who entertains a guest has them inside the home

blocks.clueFragment: Half of a B. S. Johnson book
blocks.note: the second word of Johnson's 1964 novel Albert Angelo

explanation.surface: A novel by B. S. Johnson plays host to a Californian nurse.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson's experimental novel Albert Angelo is famous for holes cut in its pages; only the second half of its title is used.
explanation.definitionFit: Angeleno is the standard name for a resident or native of Los Angeles, from the Spanish.

clue.text: The Poet Lady Charlotte a Westminster Review editor read aloud

indicators.note: reading out loud turns writing into sound, so pronunciation matters here

blocks.note: George Eliot (Mary Ann Evans) edited the Westminster Review in the 1850s

explanation.surface: A woman poet reads out the work of a journal's editor.
explanation.walkthrough: Lady Charlotte Elliot was a Victorian Scottish poet; George Eliot's surname is pronounced the same but spelt with one L and one T.
explanation.definitionFit: Lady Charlotte Elliot (1839–1880) was a Scottish poet who published under the pen-name Florenz, so this is her surname.

clue.text: Popular children flatter writer of unposted letters!

blocks.note: to fawn is to flatter servilely

explanation.surface: Well-liked children butter up an author whose letters never got sent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flatter' could be a comparative meaning more level; it is the verb. Fay Inchfawn was the pen-name of the English poet Elizabeth Rebecca Ward.
explanation.definitionFit: Fay Inchfawn wrote the collection Letters from a Lonely Woman, framed as private letters never actually mailed.

clue.text: In America producer volunteers to cut track

indicators.note: a cut goes into something, so these letters are set inside the other piece

blocks.note: the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve force

explanation.surface: An American record producer gets helpers to edit a recording.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In America' looks like a location for the producer, but it is the title of Susan Sontag's novel, which won the US National Book Award in 2000.
explanation.definitionFit: Susan Sontag wrote the historical novel In America, so she is the producer of that book.

clue.text: Curry again? It’s where Mr Bones is headed in Timbuktu

definitions.text: where Mr Bones is headed in Timbuktu

blocks.note: a balti is a curry cooked and served in a wok-like pan, a staple of British curry houses

explanation.surface: Someone groans at another curry, then explains where a character is going.
explanation.walkthrough: Mr Bones is the dog narrator of Paul Auster's novel Timbuktu, who travels with his homeless master Willy to that Maryland city.
explanation.definitionFit: In Auster's novel Willy and his dog journey to the Maryland port city to find Willy's old teacher.

clue.text: Cream cut with soprano who sang “Summertime”?

indicators.note: cutting a word short trims off its final letter

blocks.note: the cream of something is its best part

explanation.surface: A recipe involves cream diluted, alongside the soprano who sang a Gershwin aria.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summertime' is first sung by Clara in Porgy and Bess, but the heroine reprises it, which the question mark acknowledges.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of Gershwin's opera Porgy and Bess sings a reprise of the famous lullaby, so she is one singer of it.

clue.text: City set taken aback about Mr Bumble’s ass?

indicators.note: being taken aback makes one step backwards, so the order runs the other way

explanation.surface: A city is shocked by something concerning Mr Bumble's donkey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like part of the reversal signal, but it starts the definition: concerning. In Oliver Twist Mr Bumble declares 'the law is a ass'.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Bumble calls the law an ass, so anything concerning his ass relates to the law, which is what the adjective means.

clue.text: “Good always overcomes resistance” – a feminist writer

indicators.note: to overcome is to overwhelm and engulf, so one piece swallows another

blocks.note: e'er, the poetic contraction of ever

explanation.surface: A feminist author's slogan that virtue always defeats opposition.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it look like a saying by the writer; it is wordplay, with the R placed inside G plus the poetic form of 'ever'.
explanation.definitionFit: Germaine Greer, the Australian author of The Female Eunuch, is a leading figure of second-wave feminism.

clue.text: Tricky situation with cunning supplier of a staircase in Surrey!

definitions.text: supplier of a staircase in Surrey

blocks.note: to be in a stew is to be in a fix
art as craft or wiliness, as in 'arts and wiles'

explanation.surface: A crafty builder is in trouble over a staircase delivered in Surrey.
explanation.walkthrough: A Staircase in Surrey is J. I. M. Stewart's five-novel sequence set in an Oxford college, not a joinery job in the English county of Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: J. I. M. Stewart wrote the Oxford quintet titled A Staircase in Surrey, so he provided it as its author.

clue.text: Unending opera? Help!

indicators.note: with no ending, the final letter is dropped

explanation.surface: Someone stuck in an endless opera cries out for rescue.
explanation.walkthrough: Verdi's Aida is the crossword's favourite four-letter opera.
explanation.definitionFit: As nouns both mean assistance or support given to someone in need, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: EU to prosecute a male revolutionary and swineherd

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the letters are spun backwards

explanation.surface: The EU plans to put a male rebel and a pig farmer on trial.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary' seems to describe the man, but it turns round the letters after EU. Eumaeus is Odysseus's loyal servant in Homer's Odyssey.
explanation.definitionFit: In the Odyssey, Eumaeus tends Odysseus's pigs and is the first to shelter his returning master in disguise.

clue.text: “Cry ‘Havoc’ And let slip —” (Shakespeare)

blocks.note: surface reading: a command to shout for slaughter and release something, with its object missing
setter's reading: complete Mark Antony's line from Julius Caesar, Act 3

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: Antony, over Caesar's body, foresees vengeance unleashing the hounds of battle.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase personifies the violence and destruction of armed conflict as hunting hounds released from the leash.
